book_title: Chapter 3: Inside the Machine — Supply Chain, Off-Balance-Sheet Risks & Unit Economics
question: How does AMD manufacture and distribute leading-edge AI silicon without owning wafer fabs, what bottlenecks and off-balance-sheet obligations emerged in 2026, and how does $100 of FY2025 revenue convert into free cash flow?

epigraph.quote: In a capital-light fabless model, manufacturing risk does not disappear—it moves off the balance sheet into non-cancellable supplier commitments.
epigraph.author: Institutional semiconductor supply-chain principle

web_blocks.title: 3.1 Three-Tier Go-to-Market: Hyperscaler Co-Design, Tier-1 OEMs & Global Distribution

web_blocks.html: AMD's ~31,000 staff sell products through three main channels [1]. First, dedicated engineering teams sell directly to cloud giants (Microsoft, Meta, Oracle, Google, AWS) and AI labs (OpenAI, Anthropic) [1][3][6][7]. These deals involve 12-to-24-month co-design of Helios racks, liquid cooling, custom MI450 variants, and ROCm software [3][7][14]. Second, AMD sells through Tier-1 OEMs and ODMs like HPE, Dell, Lenovo, Supermicro, and Sanmina [1][3][8]. Third, global distributors like Avnet and Arrow reach thousands of industrial, embedded, and retail buyers [1].

In Item 1 of its FY2025 Form 10-K, AMD notes that normal commercial orders run on customer forecasts without binding minimums [1]. To lock in multi-gigawatt AI demand, AMD changed tactics in late 2025 and 2026. It secured binding initial 1-gigawatt commitments from OpenAI and Meta, backed by penny warrants for 160 million shares each (320 million total) [6][7]. Meanwhile, MG&A expenses were $4,144 million (12.0% of sales) in FY2025 and $3,952 million (11.2%) in 9M 2026 [1][2].

web_blocks.title: 3.2 Fabless Supply Chain: TSMC Concentration, CoWoS/HBM Bottlenecks & ATMP Partners

web_blocks.html: AMD owns zero wafer factories [1]. Instead, it relies on TSMC as its sole foundry for nearly all leading-edge CPUs, AI GPUs, and FPGAs (4nm, 3nm, and 2nm nodes) [1][14][20]. GlobalFoundries supplies older 12nm and 14nm I/O dies, while UMC and Samsung make legacy logic chips [1]. AI GPU output also faces two tight physical choke points: TSMC CoWoS packaging and HBM3E/HBM4 memory from SK Hynix, Micron, and Samsung. Each Helios rack uses 31 TB of HBM4 across 72 MI455X GPUs, so memory supply directly caps quarterly sales [14].

For final chip assembly and test (ATMP), AMD uses Asia-Pacific partners [1]. Key partners include its two Tongfu Microelectronics joint ventures (in China and Malaysia), plus SPIL and KYEC in Taiwan [1]. For full Helios racks, selling ZT Systems' factories in October 2025 made Sanmina a key capital-light rack builder [2][8]. AMD kept ZT's rack-design engineers while avoiding factory overhead [2][8]. This asset-light setup kept FY2025 continuing-ops CapEx at $974 million (2.8% of sales), though 9M 2026 CapEx rose to $1,845 million (5.2%) for internal testbeds [1][2].

web_blocks.title: 3.3 Working Capital Strain & The $81.8 Billion Off-Balance-Sheet Commitment Surge

web_blocks.html: Owning no fabs saves factory capex, yet locking in wafers and HBM4 requires heavy working capital. From year-end FY2025 to September 26, 2026, AMD's inventory jumped 44.7% from $7,920 million to $11,463 million [1][2]. Work-in-process silicon and HBM alone hit $7,416 million, while receivables rose 45.8% to $9,209 million [2]. Auditor Ernst & Young flagged Inventory Valuation as AMD's sole Critical Audit Matter in FY2025 [1]. If AI demand or export rules shift, excess stock can trigger sharp write-downs—like the ~$800 million MI308 charge in Q2 2025 [1][9].

Note 11 of the Q3 2026 Form 10-Q reveals an even bigger shift off the balance sheet [2]. Non-cancellable supplier purchase commitments quadrupled from $12,166 million at YE2025 to $48,761 million at Q3 2026 ($33.4 billion due by end of 2027) [1][2]. AMD also signed $13.3 billion in uncommenced data center leases to sublease to partners starting Q2 2027 [2]. It added $8.5 billion in maximum partner credit guarantees (up from $4.1 billion in Note 19 of FY2025 10-K) and $6,175 million in cloud compute backstops [1][2]. Private AI equity investment pledges add up to $5.1 billion, plus a $1.0 billion public equity stake in October 2026 [2]. In total, off-balance-sheet ecosystem obligations now stand near $81.8 billion [2].

web_blocks.title: 3.4 FY2025 Audited Unit Economics: $100 Revenue-to-FCF Waterfall

web_blocks.html: The waterfall below tracks every $100.00 of audited FY2025 continuing-operations revenue ($34,639 million) down to Free Cash Flow ($5,519 million, or $15.93 per $100) [1]. Consolidated CFO was $7,709 million including $1,216 million from divested ZT Manufacturing, and total CapEx was $1,012 million [1]. Using continuing operations keeps every line strictly period-matched with audited FY2025 revenue [1].

web_blocks.takeaway: Out of every $100.00 of audited FY2025 revenue, AMD retained $49.52 in GAAP gross profit, reinvested $23.36 in R&D, reported $10.66 in GAAP EBIT (depressed by $6.51 of non-cash acquisition amortization), and converted $15.93 into continuing-operations Free Cash Flow despite heavy inventory expansion.

web_blocks.mechanism: During the late-1990s fiber-optic buildout, Lucent raced to defend and win carrier share by extending billions in vendor financing, credit guarantees, and off-balance-sheet customer commitments to emerging telecom operators while ramping non-cancellable component inventories ahead of projected demand.
web_blocks.outcome_numbers: When carrier capital spending froze in 2000–2001, Lucent's revenue plunged from $38.3B (FY1999) to $21.3B (FY2001), triggering over $16.2B in FY2001 GAAP net losses, billions in bad-debt and inventory write-downs, and a forced balance-sheet restructuring that permanently impaired shareholder value.
web_blocks.lesson_for_symbol: AMD's core hyperscaler partners (Meta, Microsoft, Oracle) are vastly better capitalized than 1999 CLECs, yet AMD's 2026 pivot into $8.5B of commercial partner guarantees, $13.3B of uncommenced data center subleases, $6.2B of cloud compute backstops, and $48.8B in supplier commitments introduces classic late-cycle counterparty and inventory leverage if AI cloud utilization ever stalls.

book_paragraphs: To understand the real machinery inside AMD, you and I have to look past the silicon die and trace the money from a TSMC wafer fab all the way to a hyperscaler's liquid-cooled rack. AMD owns zero wafer factories. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company prints almost all of AMD's cutting-edge chips—from EPYC Venice server CPUs to Instinct MI450 GPUs and Xilinx FPGAs—while GlobalFoundries supplies mature 12-nanometer and 14-nanometer I/O dies. Final assembly and testing happen across Asia-Pacific at Tongfu Microelectronics joint ventures, SPIL, and KYEC, while Sanmina now handles capital-light Helios rack assembly after buying ZT Systems' factories in October 2025.

On the surface, that fabless model looks wonderfully asset-light. In fiscal 2025, AMD generated 34.6 billion dollars in revenue while spending just 974 million dollars on continuing-operations capital expenditures—barely 2.8 percent of sales. Trace every hundred dollars of FY2025 revenue down the waterfall: roughly 50 dollars and 48 cents goes to cost of sales (including 3 dollars of non-cash acquisition amortization), leaving 49 dollars and 52 cents in GAAP gross profit. AMD pours a massive 23 dollars and 36 cents into R&D and 11 dollars and 96 cents into marketing and administration. After another 3 dollars and 53 cents of acquisition amortization, GAAP operating profit lands at 10 dollars and 66 cents. Because amortization and stock-based compensation are non-cash, continuing-operations operating cash flow rises to 18 dollars and 74 cents, leaving 15 dollars and 93 cents in clean Free Cash Flow per hundred dollars of sales.

Yet here is the forensic catch that casual readers miss. When you do not own factories, risk does not vanish—it migrates into working capital and off-balance-sheet purchase commitments. To guarantee TSMC 2-nanometer wafers, CoWoS advanced packaging, and 31 terabytes of HBM4 memory per Helios rack, AMD has had to put huge chips on the table.

book_subsections.title: Walking Through the FY2025 $100 Waterfall Line by Line
paragraphs: Let's slow down and walk through every single dollar of AMD's audited FY2025 unit economics so you know exactly where the cash goes. Start with 100 dollars of continuing-operations revenue (representing 34.64 billion dollars in total FY2025 sales). First, AMD pays 47 dollars and 51 cents to TSMC for wafers, SK Hynix and Micron for HBM memory, Tongfu and SPIL for packaging, plus reserves like the second-quarter MI308 export charge. Add another 2 dollars and 98 cents of non-cash acquisition-related intangible amortization inside cost of sales, and GAAP gross profit lands at 49 dollars and 52 cents.

Next come the operating investments required to stay on the frontier of computing. AMD spends 23 dollars and 36 cents out of every 100 dollars on Research and Development—more than 8 billion dollars a year designing Zen 6 CPUs, CDNA 5 GPUs, ROCm software, and Helios racks. Marketing, general, and administrative costs take another 11 dollars and 96 cents, and non-cash intangible amortization in operating expenses removes 3 dollars and 53 cents. That leaves 10 dollars and 66 cents in GAAP operating profit.

Now watch how cash flow diverges from accounting profit. After net interest income, investment gains, and a one-time IRS tax reserve release, continuing-operations GAAP net income reaches 12 dollars and 32 cents. When we add back 6 dollars and 51 cents of non-cash intangible amortization, 4 dollars and 73 cents of stock-based compensation, and 2 dollars and 17 cents of depreciation—then subtract the cash swallowed by rising inventory and working capital—operating cash flow lands at 18 dollars and 74 cents. Subtract just 2 dollars and 81 cents for capital expenditures, and AMD keeps 15 dollars and 93 cents in clean continuing-operations Free Cash Flow per 100 dollars of sales.

book_subsections.title: Why TSMC, HBM4, and Working Capital Are the Real Bottlenecks
paragraphs: That waterfall looks healthy, yet 2026 proved that hyper-growth in AI hardware strains even a fabless cash machine. Every Helios rack requires cutting-edge 2-nanometer and 3-nanometer TSMC wafers, scarce CoWoS packaging slots, and 31 terabytes of HBM4 memory. Suppliers will not reserve that capacity on a handshake. That is why AMD's inventory swelled to 11.46 billion dollars by September 2026, accounts receivable jumped to 9.21 billion dollars, and non-cancellable supplier purchase commitments quadrupled to 48.8 billion dollars. When demand is roaring, those commitments secure supply and fuel 97 percent Data Center growth. If a macro shock or hyperscaler pause ever hits, however, non-cancellable wafer and memory orders keep arriving at the loading dock long after customer orders slow.

book_subsections.title: The $81.8 Billion Off-Balance-Sheet Web You Must Watch
paragraphs: Open Note 11 of AMD's third-quarter 2026 Form 10-Q, and the numbers should make any disciplined analyst sit up straight. In just nine months, AMD's on-balance-sheet inventory swelled 45 percent to 11.46 billion dollars—and its auditor, Ernst & Young, flagged inventory valuation as the company's sole Critical Audit Matter. Even bigger is what sits off the balance sheet.

Non-cancellable supplier purchase commitments quadrupled from 12.2 billion dollars at the end of 2025 to 48.8 billion dollars by September 2026, with 33.4 billion dollars due before the end of 2027. On top of that, AMD signed 13.3 billion dollars in 10-to-15-year data center leases meant to be subleased to commercial partners, extended up to 8.5 billion dollars in lease and debt credit guarantees, committed 6.2 billion dollars to cloud compute capacity backstops, and pledged up to 5.1 billion dollars in private AI equity investments. Add those together, and AMD now carries roughly 81.8 billion dollars in contractual and ecosystem obligations.

callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
callouts.text: History offers a sobering rhyme in Lucent Technologies between 1999 and 2001. During the fiber-optic boom, Lucent used vendor financing, credit guarantees, and massive supplier commitments to lock in equipment demand—only to absorb over 16 billion dollars in FY2001 losses when telecom capex abruptly froze. AMD's top hyperscaler partners like Microsoft, Meta, and Oracle are far stronger financially than dot-com telecom startups. Even so, whenever a fabless chipmaker takes on 81.8 billion dollars in supply, sublease, and guarantee commitments alongside 320 million customer warrant shares, you have to ask a hard question: is AMD winning pure organic pull, or is it using its balance sheet and equity to finance the ecosystem?
